issues.legal_issue: Substantial construction carried out contrary to a court’s restraint order constitutes disobedience of that order.
material_facts: A court had restrained construction on the land and required prior permission for work there.
Government reports and an expert committee’s inspection described extensive concrete and brick construction, requiring construction machinery and a large workforce.
The government acknowledged that the work had stopped by late July, and the court related the inspected construction to the period in which the restraint was in force.
issues.conclusion: The construction was substantial and was carried out in violation of the court’s orders.
issues.legal_principle: A party must obey the terms of a court order; substantial construction undertaken while an order restrains construction is a violation of that order. The court relied on its own earlier orders and the factual material, including the government’s reports and the expert committee’s report.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The matter was brought before the court as a proceeding alleging contempt.
predicates.court_order_restrained_construction: A court had ordered that construction on the land must not proceed without the court’s permission.
predicates.substantial_construction_occurred_while_: Extensive construction was carried out on the land while the restraint order remained in force.

issues.definition: When a contempt proceeding concerns extensive construction carried out while a court’s restraint on construction is in force, the construction violates the court order.

issues.legal_issue: An assurance by a minister that is presented to a court and incorporated into its order may bind both the minister personally and the government.
material_facts: The Chief Minister gave assurances at a national council meeting that the state would implement court orders concerning the land.
The assurances were recited in a Supreme Court order, and the state accepted that it remained bound by them.
The Chief Minister did not ask the court to release him from the undertaking.
issues.conclusion: The undertaking was given both personally by the Chief Minister and on behalf of the state government.
issues.legal_principle: The court treated the assurances incorporated into its order as an undertaking binding both the government and the minister personally. It relied on the terms of its earlier order and the circumstances in which the assurances were made and accepted.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The matter was brought before the court as a proceeding alleging contempt.
predicates.minister_made_assurance_of_compliance: A minister assured a public body that the government would comply with court orders.
predicates.court_incorporated_assurance_into_order: The court recorded the assurance in its order after treating it as a representation on which the order was made.

issues.definition: When a minister gives an assurance of compliance that the court incorporates into its order, the undertaking binds both the government and the minister personally.

issues.legal_issue: A government that fails to take reasonable steps to prevent disobedience of a court order may be liable for contempt.
material_facts: The state was bound by the court’s order and the undertaking recorded in the order.
Large quantities of building materials and construction equipment were brought to the site and used for extensive construction.
The government provided no account of reasonable measures taken to prevent the materials and equipment from reaching the site.
The court found no adequate basis for accepting that the government was helpless or had taken reasonable preventive steps.
issues.conclusion: The government failed to take steps to prevent the serious violation of the court’s order and was liable in contempt.
issues.legal_principle: The executive must obey judicial orders. A government cannot avoid responsibility by saying others carried out the violation if it failed to take reasonable steps to prevent it; indirect assistance or acquiescence in circumvention is also impermissible. The court relied on the undertaking recorded in its order and the principle that court orders must be obeyed.

rule.if: contempt_proceeding and government_bound_by_court_order and order_was_violated and government_failed_to_take_reasonable_preventive_steps

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The matter was brought before the court as a proceeding alleging contempt.
predicates.government_bound_by_court_order: The government was subject to a court order requiring compliance concerning the matter.
predicates.order_was_violated: Conduct occurred that contravened the court’s order.
predicates.government_failed_to_take_reasonable_pre: The government did not take reasonable measures to prevent the conduct, including by preventing necessary materials or equipment from reaching the site.

issues.definition: If a government bound by a court order fails to take reasonable steps to prevent its violation, it is liable for contempt in a contempt proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: Government departments and ministers may be proceeded against for contempt when court orders binding on them are disobeyed.
material_facts: The court’s orders and the undertaking concerned conduct by the state government and its officials.
The contempt proceedings alleged disobedience by the government and the Chief Minister.
issues.conclusion: The state government may be held liable in contempt, and a minister or government officer may be liable in an official capacity or, where a personal element contributes to the contempt, in a personal capacity.
issues.legal_principle: The contempt jurisdiction extends to government departments and ministers in their official capacities, and to individuals where their personal conduct contributes to the disobedience. The court relied on In re M. v. Home Office, (1994) 1 AC 377, and State of Bihar v. Rani Sonabati Kumari, AIR 1961 SC 221.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The matter was brought before the court as a proceeding alleging contempt.
predicates.judicial_order_binds_government_or_offic: A judicial order imposed an obligation on a government department or an official acting in an official capacity.

issues.definition: A government department or official bound by a judicial order may be proceeded against for contempt when that order is disobeyed.

issues.legal_issue: A minister who gives a personal undertaking to a court and willfully disobeys it may be convicted of contempt.
material_facts: The Chief Minister’s undertaking was both personal and on behalf of the government.
Extensive construction took place in breach of the court’s orders and undertaking.
The Chief Minister did not establish that reasonable steps had been taken to prevent the construction.
The court found a flagrant breach and willful disobedience of the undertaking.
issues.conclusion: The Chief Minister was convicted of contempt and sentenced to a token term of imprisonment and a fine.
issues.legal_principle: A minister is not immune from contempt for a personal element in disobedience of a court order. The court relied on In re M. v. Home Office, (1994) 1 AC 377, and State of Bihar v. Rani Sonabati Kumari, AIR 1961 SC 221, and applied the principle that personal responsibility attaches where the minister personally undertakes compliance and willfully disobeys.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The matter was brought before the court as a proceeding alleging contempt.
predicates.minister_personally_undertook_compliance: A minister personally undertook to the court that a court order would be obeyed.
predicates.undertaking_was_wilfully_breached: The undertaking was flagrantly disobeyed, and the minister did not establish that reasonable steps had been taken to prevent the breach.

issues.definition: When a minister personally undertakes compliance in a contempt proceeding and the undertaking is willfully breached, the minister may be convicted of contempt.
